composing_text: 69th Infantry Brigade; 151st Infantry Brigade; 231st Infantry Brigade
notes: Landed at Gold, overran 716th Division and linked with Canadians; Bayeux not taken until 7 June.
Two battalions of 56th Infantry Brigade entered Bayeux 7 June and had cleared it by noon.

current_activity: attacking toward Lingèvres and Verrières against Panzer Lehr
notes: Attacked with two brigades toward La Senaudiere, La Belle Epine, Lingevres and Verrieres 14 June; 50th Division vs Panzer Lehr continued for days.

current_activity: Bluecoat: two brigades cross the Caen-Caumont road at about 06:00 towards the Amaye-sur-Seulles feature
notes: Event date: 30 July 1944 (Ellis, vol. I, pp. 388, 389). Event definition: The division, on the left flank of XXX Corps, begins at about 06:00 to cross the main Caen-Caumont road with two brigades, each with a squadron of Shermans of the 8th Armoured Brigade, striking the junction of the German 276th and 326th Divisions; its objective is the Amaye-sur-Seulles feature near Villers-Bocage (pp. 388-389). Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. I, p. 388: "while the 50th Division secured the Amaye sur Seulles feature near Villers-Bocage on its left flank"; p. 389: "On the eastern flank two brigades of the 50th Division began to cross the main Caen—Caumont road about six in the morning". Location: Amayé-sur-Seulles, Calvados (new place) with a precision of 3 km. Location approximate: the point is Amaye-sur-Seulles, the objective; the division crossed the Caen-Caumont road some miles north-east of it. Location support: Ellis names the Amaye sur Seulles feature as the objective (p. 388).

current_activity: Market Garden: heavy mortars fire in the XXX Corps barrage; a battalion supports the Guards leaving the bridgehead
notes: Event date: 17 September 1944, from 14:30 (Ellis, vol. II, p. 32). Event definition: On the first day of Operation Market Garden, as the airborne troops finish landing, XXX Corps begins its advance from the Neerpelt bridgehead on the Meuse-Escaut canal; at 14:30 the division's heavy mortars open up, two minutes later a field artillery barrage comes down four hundred yards ahead of the front line, and as the barrage begins to move the Guards Armoured Division drives out of the bridgehead with one battalion of the division in support (p. 32). Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. II, pp. 32-33: "XXX Corps began to advance from their Neerpelt bridgehead on the canal"; "At half past two 50th Division's heavy mortars opened up". Location: Neerpelt, Limburg, Belgium (new place), the bridgehead on the canal from which XXX Corps advanced with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: the point is the village of Neerpelt; only the heavy mortars and one battalion are placed at the bridgehead, the rest of the division is not placed by the page and the division headquarters is not named. Location support: Ellis names the Neerpelt bridgehead as the place from which XXX Corps advanced and puts the division's heavy mortars and one battalion in the attack (p. 32). Commander: Maj.-Gen. D. A. H. Graham, who commanded the division to 16 October 1944 (Ellis, vol. II, p. 376). Context: Review (British Batch 2 follow-up, 28 October 2026): the row is a representative point at 0.3 because the page places only part of the division (the heavy mortars and one battalion) at the bridgehead; the division itself is not located by Ellis on 17 September.

current_activity: Nijmegen Island: holds the right of XXX Corps north of the Waal as the German attacks of early October begin
notes: Event date: 1 October 1944, taken as the first day of the attacks (Ellis, vol. II, p. 98: "October opened with more German attacks"; the attacks are not dated more closely). Event definition: In the first days of October the Germans attack north of the Waal, first the right of XXX Corps held by the division and then the left held by the 43rd Division; the American 82nd Airborne Division south-east of Nijmegen is attacked at the same time; the enemy gains some ground here and there but loses it again to counter-attacks by day or by night (p. 98). Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. II, p. 98: "October opened with more German attacks"; "North of the Waal these were first directed against XXX Corps' right held by the 50th Division". Location: Elst, Gelderland (new place), a village near the centre of the Island, the ground north of the Waal held by XXX Corps with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: the point is the village of Elst, near the middle of the Island between the Waal and the Lower Rhine; the page names the river, not a place, and the division headquarters is not named. Location support: Ellis puts the division on the right of XXX Corps north of the Waal (p. 98) and does not name the sector. Commander: Maj.-Gen. D. A. H. Graham, who commanded the division to 16 October 1944 (Ellis, vol. II, p. 376).

current_activity: II Canadian Corps takes over the Nijmegen bridgehead; the division and the 101st Airborne hold the Island
notes: Event date: 9 November 1944, noon (Stacey, p. 428). Event definition: Control of the Nijmegen bridgehead passes from the British XXX Corps to First Canadian Army and II Canadian Corps at noon on 9 November, from Cuijk to the Island; the corps has four divisions in the line: the 2nd Canadian between Cuijk and Groesbeek, the 3rd Canadian east of Nijmegen, and the 50th (Northumbrian) and the 101st United States Airborne Divisions on the Island beyond the Waal; the division is withdrawn into reserve at the end of November and replaced by the 49th (Stacey, pp. 428, 430), and Ellis, vol. II, p. 159, has it moved back to Belgium on the 29th, where it is reduced to cadre strength and then goes to the United Kingdom as a training division (the page does not name the month; read with Stacey it is 29 November). Event support: two source families (Ellis, the British official history, and Stacey, the Canadian official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. II, pp. 159-160: "On the 29th it was moved back to Belgium, where it was reduced to cadre strength"; Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 428: "Control of the Nijmegen bridgehead actually passed to First Canadian Army at noon on 9 November"; p. 430: "the 50th (Northumbrian) and 101st United States Airborne Divisions on the so-called"; p. 430: "were also withdrawn into reserve, at the end of November". Location: Elst, Gelderland (new place, see the row of 1 October 1944), a village near the centre of the Island with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: the point is the village of Elst, near the middle of the Island between the Waal and the Lower Rhine; the division sector and headquarters are not named. Location support: Stacey places the division on the so-called island beyond the Waal south of Arnhem (p. 430). Context: Commander: not recorded; Ellis, vol. II, p. 376, lists Maj.-Gen. L. O. Lyne in command from 16 October to 21 November 1944, while Stacey, p. 430, names Maj.-Gen. D. A. H. Graham, so the two histories differ and the field is left empty. The place of the move to Belgium on 29 November is not named by either history (only the country), so no separate row is written for it. Review (British Batch 2 follow-up, 28 October 2026): the Ellis page read for the move on the 29th (vol. II, p. 159) begins in the middle of the paragraph on the division, whose name is on the preceding page (p. 158), which the saved text does not contain; the division is identified from the paragraph (sent to the Middle East in April 1941, the Western Desert, Sicily, one of the first to land on D-day), from Stacey (p. 430: the 50th is withdrawn at the end of November) and from the following sentence (reduced to cadre strength, skeleton returned to the United Kingdom as a training division). The month is not named: the paragraph is a digression placed before the entry for 6 November, so on its own it would allow 29 October; 29 November is read from Stacey (p. 430: the division is withdrawn into reserve at the end of November, after II Canadian Corps took over on 9 November) and from Ellis, vol. II, p. 376 (Maj.-Gen. Graham listed again in command from 27 November 1944, so the division still existed then).
